body: For point 4, what would be in the resource for `NavigationLink`? It is entirely "local" in the sense that all data (except for the costs, and arguably layers) is only relevant for the node, the comparison would be to have a `Label` store the `text` property in a resource, it doesn't make sense to me to put anything from `NavigationLink` into a resource. Nodes like `PhysicsBody` doesn't store any similar properties like `mass` etc. in a resource

True, the navigation link in its current from probably should not have a resource attached. The point still stands for the obstacle though. Personally I would like to see more complex options for links though where the entry and exit points could be generic shapes/areas to allow marking cliffs with jump links for example.

For `NavigationObstacle` I'd say it only makes sense to put the vertices in a resource, but that's an experimental feature, but in that sense it'd be the same as `Polygon2D` which *also* doesn't store the vertices in a resource

I would say it's more similar to an Area or Collider though. Given that an obstacle would usually also have some form of collision and both of those use `Shape`s. Didn't actually know about `Polygon2D` as I have never used that before.

Both `Line2D` and `Polygon2D` are like this, they store their points in themselves and not any resource, so this is arguably the standard, as not the opposite, as `NavigationObstacle`, like `Polygon2D`, doesn't allow *arbitrary* `Shape`s, but a set of vertices, so I'd say this is *following* the norm of the engine rather than breaking any standard

The underlying issue though is that this blows up the scene files quite a bit. Especially during development when they are all stored as Text. With obstacles you will probably have quite a few that use the same shape so not being able to store them in a common resource can be quite an issue. I had to implement my own resource for this because I had scene files approaching 100mb and take way too long to load.

That's a valid point, but I'd say very much outside the scope of a discussion about aligning the navigation code with other parts, as this is not a discrepancy, I think that idea would be best as a feature proposal on its own, or it'll drown in other topics

> This could be much simpler by adding a virtual function _parse_source_geometry to Node2D and Node3D similar to

Imo this breaks locality of relevance and makes things pretty convoluted, what if you want a whole bunch of different nodes to share one behavior? How would yo make them all use the same code easily without a lot of boilerplate code? You'd also have to add it to a bunch of nodes that otherwise wouldn't have any script attached

Meanwhile you can *make* it do that by calling such a method on your node, by just making a dedicated callable for that

> Imo this breaks locality of relevance and makes things pretty convoluted, what if you want a whole bunch of different nodes to share one behavior? How would yo make them all use the same code easily without a lot of boilerplate code?

Not really seeing the issue here to be honest. The precedent has already been set with how collision data is generated and nothing is stopping you from implementing some generic parsing logic and calling that from the proposed `_parse_source_geometry` function.

```
func _parse_source_geometry(...) -> void:
 super(...)
 my_custom_parser(...)
 ...
```

```
(static) func my_custom_parser(...) -> void:
 ...
```

Is not really a lot of boilerplate. It's actually even less boilerplate than the current implementation which requires you to first allocate a parser, then set the callback and finally also take care to free that parser. Also not like the current implementation doesn't already use a similar solution as well:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/9ee1873ae1e09c217ac24a5800007f63cb895615/scene/3d/physics/static_body_3d.cpp#L153-L154
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/9ee1873ae1e09c217ac24a5800007f63cb895615/scene/3d/physics/static_body_3d.cpp#L161-L162
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/9ee1873ae1e09c217ac24a5800007f63cb895615/scene/3d/physics/static_body_3d.cpp#L145-L146
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/9ee1873ae1e09c217ac24a5800007f63cb895615/scene/3d/physics/static_body_3d.cpp#L137-L138

If anything the current implementation encourages breaking separation of concerns by allowing parsing of all kinds of different nodes in a single function no matter if they use the same logic or not. Also the current implementation does not allow you to reuse any of the existing parsing logic as it is all C++ only. I already had this issue with the previous implementation where I had to copy the code for parsing convex shapes since the code for that was private inside the `parse_source_geometry_data` function of the `NavMeshGenerator` in the navigation module. With the virtual method you would have at least access to the parent implementation. I would also argue that if your nodes have that similar parsing logic they should have a common parent.

Additionally the current implementation has one big issue and these two functions where actually what triggered me to write this issue in the first place. If I inherit from `MeshInstance3D` I can not change how my node is parsed since every parser is called for every node and this check here https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/9ee1873ae1e09c217ac24a5800007f63cb895615/scene/3d/mesh_instance_3d.cpp#L864 will be valid for any node that inherits from `MeshInstance3D`. So if I wanted to return a simplified mesh for navmesh baking I could do that but I wouldn't gain anything from that because the default parser would still be called and add the complex geometry. This is both unintuitive and inflexible.

> You'd also have to add it to a bunch of nodes that otherwise wouldn't have any script attached

Why? How would your custom nodes have any relevant parsing logic if they do not even have any custom properties? I mean sure you could contrive some esoteric example where your source geometry parser generates something based on the node name. But why would you do that externally and not in the nodes script? To throw your own words back at you "Imo this breaks locality"

If we're comparing with the physics engine it *does* use callbacks, not virtual methods, for callbacks that is, complex behavior that requires data to be fed in and out

But I can see various contexts where not calling a method on a node would make sense for the geometry parser, for example just doing something like adding extra margins or some other filtering or parsing

But a callback is the most balanced position IMO, where you can choose to call a method on the node itself, or do something else, having a virtual method on the class is IMO really limiting the flexibility
Please move to a proposal discussions. This has no qualifiers for being in the issue tracker.

> Please move to a proposal discussions. This has no qualifiers for being in the issue tracker.

This is discussing defects with the current implementation though. Not proposing any new features, I mean I guess adding the ability to replace the `NavigationServer` would count as a new feature. I would however say this very much is an issue and not a proposal even though it is indeed proposing solutions to the issues with the current implementation.

> If we're comparing with the physics engine it does use callbacks, not virtual methods, for callbacks that is, complex behavior that requires data to be fed in and out

Where exactly can I register a callback with the physics system that gets called for every node it needs a collision shape for? Cause the editor functionality to create a collision shape from a mesh is using virtual functions here:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/9ee1873ae1e09c217ac24a5800007f63cb895615/editor/plugins/mesh_instance_3d_editor_plugin.cpp#L65-L69

I would say baking a navigation mesh is pretty similar in functionality. The only callbacks in the physics server are acting on specific instances and are not generically called for every physics object registered with the server.


> But a callback is the most balanced position IMO, where you can choose to call a method on the node itself, or do something else, having a virtual method on the class is IMO really limiting the flexibility

Please give an example of where a global callback getting called for every node without any way of preventing that is somehow more flexible than a virtual function you can customize for all your custom node types. Same as the global method choosing to call a method on the node itself or not, the method on the node can choose to call a global method or not and additionally can choose to extend on the functionality already present or replace it entirely.

You are asking for extension and override exposing the NavigationServer (a major undertaking with endless amounts of longterm baggage), adding new geometry types that are completely outside of scope of navmesh that the NavigationServer is currently designed for, and other stuff causing major api breakages and new feature baggage. Maybe this is a perception problem but if that is not all clear feature proposal territory I dont know what is.

OK message received. I will stop offering advice on how to fix issues and just complain about what is not working. Clearly offering solutions is not desired by the engine team. I will also stop trying to help fix the mess that is the current navigation system because clearly you do not see any issues or are at least not interested in fixing them.

Not being able to swap out the navigation server like any other server: as intended✅ 
Storing megabytes worth of binary polygon data in a text file: nothing wrong with that ✅ 
Not being able to change the default navmesh parsing behavior of a node: working as intended ✅ 
Loading a 4mb navigation mesh takes 200 times longer than the loading the full 200mb map it was built from: perfectly fine ✅ 
Polygons in the loaded mesh get incorrectly connected: no problem ✅

You received the wrong msg.

I asked you to structure your points in a way and place where they fit so they can be discussed individually and moved forward piece by piece. The issue tracker is the wrong place for monolithic 10-things-into-one posts. Nearly each point you raise is such a big discussion point that it would deserve its entire own post.

It also has practical reasons as those single-wall-of-text posts are bound to get stuck with the majority of contributers not even finding time to read them or understanding them when they fly over 10 different topics. Not everyone is super familiar with the entire system to keep an overview what is what.

Even if more people would participate the issue template on git buries everything after a few posts. That is why everything that requires more discussions or has need for sub discussions with specific parts was moved to proposal discussions that has a better gui interface.

What I would liked to have seen is:
- Create a proposal for exposing the NavigationServer for extension.
- Create a proposal for each of all the pathfinding options that you mentioned, some may already exist (e.g. voxel).
- Create a proposal for adding multiple NavigationMeshInstances to a NavigationRegion.
- Create a proposal to move the NavigationObstacle vertices to a reusable data resource.
- Create a proposal discussion for the source geometry parser to discuss the pros and cons and why things are as they are.
- ...

You can still do that and help actually move things forward.

Yes and by the point that gets anywhere the source parsing api will have been moved from beta to release and it gets even harder to change anything. You have already changed the navmesh baking process multiple times and now you are releasing a new one directly into a beta release without any prior testing.

I created an issue about `sync` having abysmal performance, told you why that was the case and how you could solve the problem. You told me to open a proposal for that. That is an obvious defect. There is no need to propose anything. If your code is so horrendously slow that loading everything else of a level is 100-200x faster there is an obvious defect in your implementation. Especially if the reference implementation (detours) can do it 1000x faster than yours.

I created an issue telling you that sync incorrectly connects the polygons, why that was the case and how you could fix the issue. Again you told me to open a proposal for that because apparently correcting the polygons correctly is not in the spec? Or why do you want a proposal for an obvious bug?

Now you introduce new functionality with obvious drawbacks in a beta release without any prior testing. I open an issue to try and prevent that from going live and yet again you tell me to open a proposal.

If you ask for advice I will be happy to give it, but I will no longer proactively offer it while I have the feeling it just leads to the underlying issue getting ignored.

@0x0ACB I sense that there's a lot of frustration in your last message. I understand that contributing and participating in an open source project can get frustrating at times. Especially when things aren't going the way we would want to. Trust me, it happened a lot to me too (and to all of us also). But that's why the project has a code of conduct.

I just want to cite here two of the expectations of the [Godot code of conduct](https://godotengine.org/code-of-conduct/). I added emphasis.

> Feedback is always welcome but **keep your criticism constructive**. We encourage you to open discussions, proposals, issues, and bug reports. Use the community platforms to discuss improvements, **not to vent out frustration**. Similarly, when other users offer you feedback **please accept it gracefully**.

and

> **Always assume positive intent from others.** Be aware that differences in culture and English proficiency make written communication more difficult than face-to-face communication and that your interpretation of messages may not be the one the author intended. Conversely, if someone asks you to rephrase something you said, be ready to do so without feeling judged.

I'm not a navigation specialist, but from what I understand, your issue was bound to be closed. What would be the expected result of such an issue? That we completely stall the 4.4 release until we refactor the entire navigation stack? This will not happen.

Your issue reads more like a rant than an actual issue, which is not constructive at all.

Though, for the sake of this exercise, let's just assume that it's not a rant.

> Yes and by the point that gets anywhere the source parsing api will have been moved from beta to release and it gets even harder to change anything.

I don't understand here the urgency. I can assure you that we will not refactor the entire NavigationServer before the 4.4 release, nor will postpone the release date until said refactor is done. The project doesn't work that way.

We are already in beta, it means that we are in feature freeze. No major refactor nor new feature will make it to 4.4.

> You have already changed the navmesh baking process multiple times and now you are releasing a new one directly into a beta release without any prior testing.

I trust here that @smix8 did everything they could before merging the changes. Please note that it is also a team effort, as there's a release management thing supervising every changes to the engine.

I highly encourage you to submit targeted issues if the changes break your project performance-wise. That way, we can assess the issue individually, and make the best decision.

> I created an issue about sync having abysmal performance, told you why that was the case and how you could solve the problem. You told me to open a proposal for that.

Please note that https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/96483 and https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/100759 aren't what I call targeted issues. They contain assessments on the quality of the code and feel a lot like a rant, instead of focusing on the objective issues at hand.

If you can make assessment on the quality of the code, I highly suggest to start taking the one issue at a time and doing small PRs in order to participate in collegiality. Telling people how to solve the issue isn't usually constructive.

> There is no need to propose anything. If your code is so horrendously slow that loading everything else of a level is 100-200x faster there is an obvious defect in your implementation. Especially if the reference implementation (detours) can do it 1000x faster than yours.

Here, you're doing code assessments and you're taking things personal ("your code is so horrendously slow", "obvious defect in your implementation", "1000x faster than yours").

I suggest you to create a PR implementing that 1000x optimization instead of telling @smix8 to do it. @smix8 isn't bound to do what you tell them to do.

> I created an issue telling you that sync incorrectly connects the polygons, why that was the case and how you could fix the issue. Again you told me to open a proposal for that because apparently correcting the polygons correctly is not in the spec? Or why do you want a proposal for an obvious bug?

No, you created an issue titled "`NavigationServer3D::sync` could be optimized". And also, if your suggestion would lead to a complete refactor of the current system, yes, this warrants a proposal and cannot be considered a bug. 

A bug is a system not working properly due to a defect. And no, known limitations cannot be assimilated to a "bug".

A blender not being able to bake waffles is not a bug, it's just that a blender is not meant to bake waffles.

> Now you introduce new functionality with obvious drawbacks in a beta release without any prior testing.

Again, I trust that @smix8 did everything necessary beforehand. 

If you find actual issues, like regressions between 4.4.dev7 and 4.4.beta1, I highly encourage you to create individual and targeted issues.

>  I open an issue to try and prevent that from going live and yet again you tell me to open a proposal.

Broad and vague issues titled like this one ("Navigation design does not align with the rest of the engine") will never prevent features from going stable. Only actual, targeted, and constructive issues about actual regressions will.

> If you ask for advice I will be happy to give it, but I will no longer proactively offer it while I have the feeling it just leads to the underlying issue getting ignored.

What we're all trying to tell you right now is that the way you're "offering" advice is not constructive.

--------

Even in your rants, it seems that there's some good ideas in there. We highly encourage you to focus on more specific issues and even to create (small) PRs instead of telling people how to do things.

(I say small PRs because complete refactors of systems that come out-of-the-blue aren't usually merged.)
